sample/ask: A model answers a question by sampling. Asked seven times eight, it says fifty six half the time, fifty four three times in ten, and sixty four the rest.
sample/reward: A checker scores each answer: a reward, R, of one when it is right and zero when it is wrong. It is just a number, with nothing to differentiate.
sample/goal: Training should raise the expected reward: the average R over the model's answers, here zero point five. Its gradient would say how to change the parameters, theta.
sample/stuck: But theta reaches the reward only through which answer gets sampled, and a random draw has no slope.
trick/sum: Write the expected reward as a sum over answers: each answer's probability times its reward. Only the probabilities depend on theta.
trick/trick: Now the trick. The slope of log pi is the slope of pi divided by pi. So the gradient of pi is pi times the gradient of its log.
trick/avg: Put that in, and the gradient of the expected reward becomes a sum of pi times R times the gradient of log pi: an average over the model's own answers.
trick/est: So sample one answer, and multiply its reward by the gradient of its log-probability. That one sample is an estimate of the gradient: the policy gradient.
trick/eg: For fifty six, this model's gradient of log pi is zero point five, minus zero point three, minus zero point two. With R equal to one, the estimate is that same vector.
push/up: Step theta a little along the estimate, and the log-probability of the sampled answer rises, in proportion to R. A rewarded fifty six becomes more likely.
push/zero: A wrong answer gets R of zero, so its estimate is zero, and nothing moves.
push/neg: A negative reward flips the step, and makes that answer less likely.
push/loss: As a loss to minimize, it is minus R times log pi of the sample: cross-entropy on the model's own answer, weighted by its reward.
